# The Object That Could Not Be Wrong

For 130 years, a kilogram was a particular thing. Not a kind of thing, but one thing: a cylinder of platinum and iridium, small enough to hide in a fist, kept under three nested bell jars in a vault in Sèvres, outside Paris. Opening the vault took three keys held by three different people. Officially the cylinder was the International Prototype of the Kilogram; unofficially it was Le Grand K. It had a property no other object on Earth shared: it could not weigh the wrong amount.

That is a statement about logic, not craftsmanship. The kilogram was defined as the mass of this cylinder, so whatever its mass happened to be, that was one kilogram. If someone scratched it and a few atoms came away, the cylinder did not become lighter than a kilogram. Everything else in the universe became slightly heavier. Your body, the moon, the Andromeda galaxy would all be revised upward, on paper, by a scratch.

Wittgenstein noticed this about the kilogram's sibling: "There is one thing of which one can say neither that it is one metre long, nor that it is not one metre long, and that is the standard metre in Paris." A standard is not measured. It is what measuring means.

The trouble was the copies. Six official duplicates lived in the vault alongside the prototype, and dozens more were distributed to national laboratories around the world. Three times, in 1889, in the 1940s, and around 1990, the copies were brought back and compared with the original. They had drifted. Over a century, the copies and the prototype diverged by about fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a grain of fine sand.

I love the predicament this created. Either the copies had gained mass or the prototype had lost it, and there was no way to tell which, because a comparison gives only differences. Most likely all of them were drifting, including the prototype, in some common direction that no comparison could reveal. The metrologists knew something was wrong, and their own definition forbade them from saying what. The one object that might have been the culprit was the one that was innocent by decree.

The irony is that the metric system was invented to escape exactly this. The French revolutionaries who designed it wanted units taken from nature rather than from a king's foot, units "for all time, for all people." The metre would be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and the kilogram would be the mass of a litre of water. Two astronomers, Delambre and Méchain, spent seven years surveying the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, through a revolution and a war, and were periodically arrested as spies for carrying strange instruments up church towers. Méchain found a discrepancy in his own data, concealed it, and was tormented by it until he died.

Then the results were cast in platinum, and the platinum quietly took over. You cannot carry the Earth into a workshop to check a ruler. In practice the bar was the metre and the cylinder was the kilogram, and when later surveys showed the bar was about a fifth of a millimetre short of its planetary ideal, nobody changed the bar. Nature was the aspiration, but the artifact was the reality.

The metre broke free first. In 1960 it was redefined by a wavelength of krypton light, and in 1983 as the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The trick is that nobody measures the speed of light anymore. Its value is fixed by fiat, exactly, forever, and the metre is whatever length makes that number come out right.

The kilogram held out until 2019, because mass is harder. The eventual solution was the Kibble balance, a machine that weighs an object against an electromagnetic force, which quantum effects tie to Planck's constant. It took decades to make these machines agree to within a few parts in a hundred million. When they did, delegates from around the world gathered at Versailles and voted. As of May 20, 2019, Planck's constant is exactly 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds, and a kilogram is whatever makes that true.

In one sense, nothing changed. The new definition was tuned to match the old one, so no bathroom scale noticed. What moved was the uncertainty. Before, the cylinder was exact and Planck's constant was known only approximately. Now the constant is exact and the cylinder is approximate. For the first time in its existence, Le Grand K has a mass that can be measured, and it can be off.

I find that demotion oddly moving. The cylinder is still there, under its jars in its vault, but now it is only an object, a very carefully made piece of metal weighing about a kilogram, give or take. It had been a definition and became a datum.

The revolutionaries finally got their wish, 220 years late. The kilogram now belongs to all times and all peoples in the strongest sense. A laboratory on another planet with no contact with Earth could reconstruct it from physics alone. Nothing needs to be shipped from Paris, and nothing can be scratched, stolen, or bombed.

But something was traded away, and I think it's worth saying what. The old definition could be explained to a six-year-old: a kilogram is how heavy that thing is. The new one requires quantum mechanics even to state. We exchanged a standard anyone could understand but only one vault could hold for a standard anyone can reproduce but almost no one can understand. I think that was the right trade, though it is still a trade.

What stays with me is that there was never an option to fix nothing. To measure anything, something has to be held still by declaration, placed beyond question so that everything else can be questioned against it. The only choice is what to fix. For a century we chose a lump of metal and lived with the absurdity that it could not be wrong. Now we have chosen a number woven into the structure of the universe, and the lump of metal is free, at last, to drift.

I'm settling on the kilogram as the subject: the platinum-iridium cylinder that defined mass for over a century before 2019, and the Kibble balance and Planck constant that replaced it. The idea that the old prototype couldn't be wrong, since any drift in its mass simply meant the universe had gotten heavier, is the point I want the essay to turn on.

I'm now drafting the opening: a kilogram as one specific object, a platinum-iridium cylinder kept under bell jars in a Sèvres vault and opened with three keys, and the idea that it could not weigh the wrong amount.

I'm checking whether the cylinder's mass really matters for the definition: it's the reference, so whatever it weighs is the kilogram, and any scratch would make the rest of the universe heavier rather than the cylinder lighter. Then there's the Wittgenstein remark about the standard metre in Paris, which fits the same logic. The next thing I need to deal with is the copies, of which there were six sisters kept in the vault and dozens of national ones distributed elsewhere.

I'm noting that the copies drifted relative to the prototype by roughly fifty micrograms over a century, and that no one can tell whether the copies gained or the original lost, since only differences can be measured. That leaves metrologists sure something was off while the definition barred them from saying what.

Now I'm weighing how the metre slipped loose before the kilogram did, since it was redefined first, in 1960, by a wavelength of krypton light.

I'm working out how the metre lost its physical anchor first, with light's speed fixed by definition in 1983, which left the kilogram as the last holdout until the Planck constant took over.

I'm settling on the kilogram's trade-off now: the new Planck-based definition fixes the constant exactly and leaves the cylinder as just an object with a measurable, imperfect mass, which feels like a quiet demotion. It's open to anyone in principle, even a civilization elsewhere, yet it's far harder to grasp than "the weight of this thing."

I'm also checking that the cylinder is still kept in the vault and will be checked from time to time, so the closing image can rest on that.
